NUT 1800.d: This course identifies and discusses career options and market trends within the fields of nutrition, dietetics, and food service management. It reviews the academic and professional requirements for successful entry into these fields.

NUT 2040.d: This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the fundamental concepts of human nutrition, including digestion, absorption, metabolism, and the function of nutrients as they relate to human health and disease.

NUT 2060.d: Students learn about the food system, how food is delivered in the United States, and the concept of justice in food. Students explore how Social Determinants of Health interact with our food system and how that interaction results in food injustice. NUT 3000.d: In this course, the science of nutrition is explored within a historical context. Students learn how ideas and practices related to food, nutrition, agriculture and food technology shift in different times and places, beginning with prehistoric times and continuing through the 20th century. This class examines how the concept of nutrition itself has changed over time and how those changes have affected what societies and individuals consume, and how this impacts nutrition-related disease trends seen in modern day.

NUT 3040.d: This course provides additional study of the chemistry and biochemistry of nutrients, metabolic functions in health and disease, food composition, digestion, absorption, and nutrient utilization with a focus on how these concepts relate to current nutrition topics being discussed in the popular press. This course is intended for non-nutrition majors.

NUT 3050.d: This course is designed to increase the non-nutrition major's knowledge of the physiological, psychological, sociological, and cultural factors which influence nutritional needs and eating habits throughout the life cycle. Nutrient requirements, dietary planning guidelines, and techniques for assessing nutritional status will be presented for the following life stages: preconception, pregnancy, lactation, infancy, childhood, adolescence, and aging.

NUT 3101.d: Body image concerns too often inhibit women's, men's, and non-binary people's health and productivity. Like any challenge, these also hold potential for stimulating personal and civic transformation. In this course, students from all backgrounds explore the genetic, developmental, social, cultural, technological, and geopolitical factors affecting perceptions of healthy weight, size, and body image. They engage with evidence-based behavior change theories, strategies, and activities. These expand their capacity for promoting healthy behaviors and productive perspectives in diverse settings including families, schools, sports, college, workplaces, healthcare, social media, and other types of communities.

Rating: Low.
NUT 3110.d: In this course, students are introduced to foods as chemical systems; structure-function relationships of water, protein, lipids, carbohydrates, minerals, and natural products in foods; food safety fundamentals; preservation and preparation methods and effects on food quality.

Rating: Low.
NUT 3150.d: Students learn about human digestion, absorption, metabolism, and health effects of macronutrients, water, and alcohol in this course. Also included are basic concepts of energetics, electrolytes, artificial sweeteners, and fiber.

NUT 3160.d: Students learn about human digestion, absorption, metabolism, and health effects of micronutrients in this course. Students also learn about basic concepts of the Dietary Reference Intakes, phytochemicals, supplements, microbiome, epigenetics, and nutrigenomics.

NUT 3300.d: Students will learn about global cultural, social, and political systems that determine the nutritional status and well-being of global communities. Students will develop an understanding of key social and behavioral science concepts for exploring global nutrition trends and problems. Through study of existing social science models, current research, and analysis of government data, students will apply theories to develop action plans for specific regions that consider global positioning and status.

NUT 3310.d: This course is about the nutrition of Mexican citizens living in Mexico, as well as Mexican immigrants and Mexican Americans living in the United States. Over a decade, AI-mediated virtual immersion — real-time translation, AI travel guides, simulated cultural exchange — will be far more capable and could chip away at some preparatory or reflective components of study-abroad pedagogy. NUT 3320.d: This is a variable topics course conducted in a study abroad format. The countries visited will vary as to where the course is offered. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating AI-generated global-health claims against behavioral-science frameworks — a verification function — rather than toward not needing the course. The rating rises to Medium: exposed analytical tasks meet a durable but non-course-specific institutional mandate that a purely elective course would lack.

A decade out, AI is plausibly capable of generating sophisticated global-nutrition assessments integrating demographic, agricultural, and health data, consistent with rapid capability growth trends and the roughly four-to-seven-month doubling of AI task-time horizons. The underlying analytical tasks are substantially automatable by this horizon in the central case. Yet the general-studies designation persists absent statewide gen-ed policy change, keeping the course required regardless of surrounding AI capability, and evaluating population-health claims for soundness remains a critical-thinking competence the evidence base treats as durable. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by the transfer mandate. The uncertainty concerns how the course assesses analytical skill under ubiquitous AI synthesis tools, not whether the general-education requirement and underlying need for global-health reasoning persist through 2036.

The rating moves to Medium: content generation is increasingly automatable, but the general-education mandate and the underlying critical-analysis competence together prevent full erosion.

A decade out, AI-generated cultural and anthropological analysis of food will be sophisticated and widely available, substantially eroding the rationale for students to produce such analysis unaided, consistent with the fast capability trajectory the evidence base documents. But the general-studies designation persists in the central case absent statewide transfer-policy change, and the human capacity for socially and politically situated critical reasoning about food systems retains value the evidence base treats as resistant to full automation. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by the institutional mandate. NUT 3375.d: This course is an exploration of how food procurement, dietary practices, ideologies of consumption, and food celebrations across cultures are related to varying environments, subsistence strategies, moral sensibilities, socioeconomic and political conditions, social identities, and social hierarchies. Using an anthropological approach, students examine how the ideological, emotional, symbolic, aesthetic, and social value of food and its marketing varies across cultures. NUT 3400.d: This course is a study of the basic principles of, and latest trends in, weight management. This course includes coverage of assessment techniques, behavioral and non-behavioral treatment approaches and prevention strategies. The concept of "health at every (body) size" will be presented. Fad diets and programs with sound nutrition principles will be analyzed.

r: Food Safety covers the toxicology and microbial and non-microbial contamination of food and dietary supplements — sources of contamination, prevention and control methods, detection techniques, and the beneficial role of certain microbes. The content-area accreditation tie for food-science competency in the dietetics curriculum caps erosion at Medium regardless of how well AI explains the science. A decade out, AI food-safety analysis and hazard detection will be considerably more capable, plausibly assisting real contamination-detection workflows in industry as diffusion continues past its current modest adoption rate among firms. But the pedagogical function here — a nutrition or food-science student personally acquiring the judgment to evaluate contamination risk and interpret detection results — is not eliminated by that trend, and the accreditation-linked content requirement persists absent a change to dietetics program standards. The rating holds Medium, capped by verification burden and the content mandate from reaching High even as raw capability keeps climbing. The uncertainty concerns how much routine hazard detection industry automates around a still-human safety-judgment core, not whether food-safety literacy remains instrumentally necessary for students entering nutrition and dietetics practice.
NUT 3500.d: This course covers the safety and toxicology of food and dietary supplements with respect to microbial and non-microbial contamination. Sources of contamination, ways to prevent or control contamination, consequences of contamination and methods of detection are covered. Beneficial aspects of microbes in food with respect to human health are also discussed.

The rating holds Low. The uncertainty concerns how much documentation and pre-session preparation automates around a still-human counseling core, not whether nutrition majors still need to personally develop live counseling delivery skill.
NUT 3700.d: The student will be prepared to participate in the specialized communications of nutrition professionals. Students will practice preparing, conducting, and analyzing group nutrition education, individual nutrition counseling, and healthcare team communications. Written communication guided by the nutrition care process will also be covered. This course is designed for nutrition majors.

r: This one-credit course trains students to critically evaluate nutrition, health, and wellness claims embedded in documentary films and books, weighing evidentiary quality, source motive, and scientific validity. Task-exposure research finds writing- and analysis-adjacent activities among the more exposed categories even where critical thinking is nominally involved, because the underlying operation is pattern-matching across text rather than embodied judgment. Observed-usage data already shows writing and analytical tasks as a dominant share of everyday AI use, and that diffusion should be considerably broader by five years given the pace of capability growth documented in compute and task-horizon trend research. Verification burden here is moderate rather than severe: a misjudged nutrition claim in a documentary is not immediately dangerous, so the threshold for trusting an AI-generated critique is lower than in clinical contexts. With no accreditation lock, general-studies mandate, or foundational role protecting it, the instrumental case for a dedicated course teaching students to do this evaluative work by hand substantially erodes, even as the underlying media-literacy skill stays valuable.

The instrumental rationale for a stand-alone one-credit course teaching this evaluative skill is substantially diminished under that scenario, since neither embodiment, verification stakes, foundational sequencing, nor an institutional mandate holds it in place. The hedge is genuine: forecasting a full decade of media ecosystems and misinformation dynamics is uncertain, and a resurgence of demand for demonstrably human-verified critique in an AI-saturated information environment is plausible. But absent that shift, and consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing- and text-analysis-heavy work is among the more exposed categories, this rating holds High; the course's disciplinary and civic value is untouched by this instrumental read, which concerns only whether AI performs the task.
NUT 3800.d: An examination of nutrition, health, and wellness messages in contemporary documentary films and books. The course will focus on critical analysis and evaluation to determine the validity and reliability of messages in documentary films and books.

The verification burden is moderate; a wrong judgment about an influencer's credibility carries real but not acute harm, so the threshold for relying on automated evaluation is comparatively low. With no institutional lock or foundational role shielding it, the instrumental case for teaching students to perform this specific evaluative task by hand substantially erodes. The rating rises to High; the residual value is in cultivating a habit of skepticism, which this instrumental reading does not score.

A decade out, the central case has AI-native tools performing continuous, well-calibrated evaluation of nutrition claims across whatever social platforms exist by 2036, likely surfacing corrections and credibility scores automatically rather than requiring a student to learn manual evaluation techniques. Nothing in this course's structure, no embodiment, no accreditation tie, no prerequisite dependency, offers protection against that trajectory, and task-exposure research's consistent finding that text-based evaluative work sits toward the exposed end of the spectrum supports a High rating here as well. The genuine hedge is that social media itself, and the misinformation dynamics this course addresses, could look unrecognizably different by 2036, and a countervailing demand for demonstrably human media literacy in an AI-saturated feed is plausible. Absent that shift, the instrumental need for a dedicated course teaching this specific skill is substantially diminished, even as the underlying literacy goal retains real civic value.
NUT 3810.d: This course examines nutritional messaging in social media. It covers critical thinking skills in evaluating validity of nutritional messaging. Students will explore different social media platforms, how nutrition stories are presented, and best practices for identifying if the sources are trustworthy.

NUT 3820.d: The course examines vegan and vegetarian diets. Students will explore why vegan and vegetarian diets are chosen for heath, social, environmental, religious or other reasons. NUT 3850.d: In this course, relationships between nutrition and chronic disease on an individual, group and/or population-level will be explored. NUT 3910.d: This course is designed to increase the students' knowledge in the area of breastfeeding support. By 2031, AI tools will likely assist internship placements with documentation, scheduling, or preliminary analysis tasks depending on the specific site, but the defining requirement of this course, a student physically performing supervised professional work under faculty and site oversight, is not something a model performs on the student's behalf. Verification burden is high because internship performance is directly evaluated against real professional standards, and embodiment keeps the applied work resistant to substitution regardless of how capable AI becomes at adjacent informational tasks. Supervised-practice requirements feeding dietetics credentialing pathways change on slow, accreditation-driven cycles and are unlikely to relax within one or two catalog revisions. The rating stays Low: the internship's instrumental necessity is preserved by the combination of embodied placement and the credentialing structure it feeds, even as AI reshapes the informational tasks a student encounters on site.

Even under an aggressive central-case capability scenario, a decade does not plausibly dissolve the requirement that Human Nutrition-Dietetics majors complete supervised, in-person professional practice before proceeding toward credentialing; accreditation-linked supervised-practice requirements in health fields are characteristically slow-moving, changing on multi-year cycles rather than in response to a single capability jump. The embodied core of the internship, performing real professional tasks under direct supervision, sits at the intersection of low task-exposure and durable institutional lock-in, and nothing in the available evidence suggests AI substitutes for accruing that experience by 2036. The genuine uncertainty concerns how AI tools reshape the day-to-day informational and documentation tasks within a given placement, not whether the supervised placement itself remains required. The rating holds Low with reasonable confidence, anchored jointly by embodiment and by the credentialing pathway this internship experience feeds.
NUT 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly draft comprehensive community nutrition assessments, program plans, and educational materials with a competence approaching what this course currently trains students to produce by hand, and the productivity gains documented for professional writing and planning tasks generally support that trajectory. Verification burden is moderate rather than severe, a flawed program plan is correctable before harm occurs, unlike a clinical misjudgment, so the threshold for trusting AI-drafted public-health materials is comparatively low. The course's partial contribution to broader program accreditation expectations offers only modest inertia, not a binding cap, since no course-specific mandate or foundational role protects it. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a dedicated course to teach manual execution of these tasks substantially erodes, even as public-health nutrition judgment retains disciplinary value outside this instrumental reading.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently performing most of the assessment, program-planning, and policy-synthesis work this course's knowledge is applied to, integrated into public-health nutrition workflows much as it has diffused into adjacent administrative fields. With no accreditation-specific mandate, foundational scaffolding role, or embodiment protecting this course, little holds back the erosion task-exposure research would predict for administrative and writing-heavy work of this kind. The rating is High, hedged by genuine uncertainty over how public-health institutions adopt AI tools at the pace capability suggests, given the macro evidence that diffusion consistently lags capability. The residual human role plausibly concentrates in community-specific judgment, stakeholder relationships, and legislative advocacy that resist full automation, but the instrumental case for the course as currently structured is substantially diminished under the central-case scenario.
NUT 4000.d: This course concerns the nutritional status of individuals, families, households, communities, and populations. Topics covered include health and nutrition assessment, programs and resources, legislation, education, and program planning as they impact nutrition and public health.

By 2031, AI application assistants will plausibly handle most of what this course teaches directly, tracking DICAS requirements and deadlines, drafting and iterating personal statements, and matching a student's profile to suitable Dietetic Internship programs, with a fluency that exceeds what a one-credit course can teach through instruction alone. With no institutional lock-in or scaffolding role, the instrumental case continues to erode. The rating stays High: this is close to a best-case scenario for automation given fully digital, low-verification, administrative work with no protective structural factor, though demand for the course's advising function may persist independent of this instrumental read.

A decade out, AI-assisted application preparation for graduate and professional programs is plausibly a mature, ubiquitous consumer capability, and the specific administrative tasks this course addresses, researching programs, navigating DICAS, assembling documents, are about as automatable as any task in this evidence base: fully digital, low verification burden, no embodiment, no accreditation mandate, and no foundational role. The rating is High with reasonable confidence, tempered only by the standard ten-year hedge that application systems and internship-matching processes themselves could be restructured in ways that change what students need help with. The course's continuing value, if any, would lie in advising relationships and support through a competitive process rather than in teaching the mechanical application-preparation tasks the description centers on, which sit outside this instrumental rating's scope.
NUT 4010.d: The majority of students studying Nutrition will go on to apply for a Dietetic Internship program. The system used by students to apply for Dietetic Internship programs is called the Dietetic Internship Centralized Application System (DICAS). There are many moving parts to filling out a DICAS application which can make it a complicated process. Additionally, there are hundreds of Dietetic Internship programs to choose from. This class would assist students in researching Dietetic Internship programs, navigating DICAS, and preparing all necessary documents in order to have a competitive and complete application.

The residual, judging whether a study design is appropriate to a research question, or whether a statistical result is being over-interpreted, is real but considerably narrower than the course's full execution-oriented content, and the program's accreditation-linked research-literacy expectation no longer caps the rating meaningfully beyond the near term. The rating is High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how much human oversight nutrition research retains given publication and ethical-review structures that may sustain more human involvement than a pure capability read suggests. Confidence is moderate: the directional erosion is clear even though the residual footprint of human-led research design a decade out is harder to pin down precisely.
NUT 4040.d: Understanding that modern research design and evaluation rarely occur alone and that nutrition professionals will be expected to collaborate with other members of a healthcare and/or research team, this course will provide students with an advanced and practical understanding of applied research design and evaluation in the field of nutrition. Topics include integrating the process of conducting research with study design principles, statistical analysis, qualitative and quantitative methods, research report development, dissemination of research findings and research ethics.

No general-studies designation locks it into the general-education core, though its cultural-competency content plausibly contributes to the program's broader accreditation expectations. At 24 months, that mix yields meaningful but partial erosion. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will more capably synthesize global nutrition epidemiology, historical and economic context, and even simulate cross-cultural communication scenarios for practice, further narrowing the informational core this course delivers. Observed-usage data already shows explanatory and cross-cultural informational tasks well represented in everyday AI use, and that diffusion should widen further given the documented pace of capability growth. Verification burden is moderate, misunderstanding a cultural or epidemiological detail is correctable rather than acutely dangerous in the course's own setting, so the threshold for AI-assisted delivery of this content is comparatively low. The course's contribution to broader accreditation-linked cultural-competency expectations offers only modest, non-binding inertia. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for teaching this global-nutrition knowledge base primarily through direct human instruction substantially erodes, even as applied client-facing cultural competence retains practical value outside this reading.

A decade out, the central case has AI delivering sophisticated, personalized instruction in global nutrition epidemiology, food ethics, and cross-cultural context, and even supporting simulated practice of culturally appropriate counseling strategies, with the course's foundational-knowledge rationale substantially eroded under that scenario. No hard institutional mandate, deep foundational-scaffolding role, or strong embodiment factor holds the rating down at this horizon. The hedge is genuine: global nutrition realities, migration patterns, and food systems could shift substantially by 2036 in ways that change what cultural competence actually requires, and real client-facing counseling practice, as distinct from the knowledge base this course conveys, may retain more protection than the informational content alone. The rating is High with that caveat, consistent with task-exposure research's classification of explanatory, cross-cultural informational content as comparatively exposed relative to embodied clinical practice.
NUT 4050.d: This course focuses on equipping students to work with diverse populations and provides students with a foundation of knowledge concerning historical, social, and economic factors driving global nutrition. The current and future state of global nutrition will be discussed along with historical and future methods for addressing global malnutrition. Topics include epidemiology of nutritional diseases and malnutrition, sustainable agriculture, ethics in food, analyzing cross-cultural communication skills, identifying and utilizing culturally appropriate strategies in counseling and client care, and exploring various cultural traditions.

NUT 4060.d: This course provides students with an opportunity to examine and apply strategies and principles of effective communication for diverse audiences in the field of nutrition. Emphasis will be placed on effective translation and dissemination of scientific findings to diverse audiences using a variety of communication strategies including individual counseling, group facilitation, advocacy, and public speaking. The evaluation, interpretation, and communication of scientific literature will also be emphasized.

NUT 4160.d: This course will introduce students to leadership concepts including: different leadership theories, leadership skills, diversity and inclusion, human resources, and more. NUT 4200.d: This course is designed to increase the nutrition major's knowledge about the physiological, psychological, sociological, and cultural factors which influence nutritional needs and eating habits throughout the life cycle with a focus on evidence-based practices. NUT 4700.d: This course examines principles and application of medical nutrition therapy as related to specific disease states. Topics include the nutrition care process, nutrition assessment, nutrition support, and therapeutic diets.
